title: Tenths Builder
context: Grade 5, the first pages on tenths. An adult sees a fraction written a new way. What the pages are doing is cutting one whole into ten equal parts, naming one part a tenth, and writing wholes and tenths either side of a point, with ten tenths making one whole. The opening box's question can be counted in tenths; the child does that with its own numbers, and no one answers it for them.

writeup.why: Write tenths of a whole, and wholes with tenths, as fractions and as decimals, and trade ten tenths for one whole to count lots of tenths into ones and tenths.
writeup.look: Strips of one length stacked across the working area, a fraction card and a decimal card to their right, and Cut, Shape, Trade and Lots of buttons under them.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Tenths Builder' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x sixty-four, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many tenths are shaded in all, counting ten for each whole strip. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x sixty-four, y 202. The strips lie across the working area, each 900 long and 60 tall, their left ends at x 110, stacked from y 250 downward with 20 between them, each labelled Whole in ink at its left. The part strip is always the lowest. Its ten parts are exactly one width, cut by near-black lines; shaded parts are deep blue and unshaded parts warm white. On the Shape switch the part strip becomes a circle 260 across at x 380, y 460, cut into ten equal sectors. The fraction card and the decimal card stand at x 1030, y 300, one above the other, the decimal card with a large near-black point and the words Whole number part and Decimal part under its two sides. The Cut, Shape, Trade and Lots of buttons sit in a row along the bottom of the working area at y 670, each labelled in words. When ten tenths are traded they slide together, their cut lines fading to half strength, and the strip closes with a vermilion flash labelled Trade. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across with a point key and a fraction bar key, for setting a number of tenths up to ninety-nine, or for typing a fraction or a decimal into the answer slot. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the tools of this chapter share them. A decimal or fraction the question gives is deep blue, with the shaded parts that show it. The result the working reaches, a decimal, a fraction, a sum, a difference or what is left, is green, with its shaded parts. Ten of one place traded for one of the next, a carry in adding or a trade in taking away, is vermilion. A zero written after the point to line decimals up is violet, and so is the point written after a whole number before those zeros. The part taken away, used or poured out is rose. The digit, place or step being worked on now, and the first place where two decimals differ, are amber. A zero holding a place open inside a number is grey, and nothing else on the stage is ever grey. An unshaded part stays warm white inside its near-black outline, the decimal point is near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey. Chrome never borrows one of them, and each of those readings survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label, Given, Answer, Carry, Trade, Added zero, Taken away, Left or Place holder, before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last count of tenths as whole strips and a part strip, with its decimal written under them.

phases.win: the fraction card shows 1/10, the decimal card shows 0.1 in green, and the voice reads zero point one
phases.does: taps Cut, checks that the ten parts are one width, and shades one part
phases.goal: a whole cut into ten equal parts gives tenths, and one part is 1/10, written 0.1
phases.says: Cut the strip into ten equal parts. Shade one. What is it called?
phases.check: Away from the screen: if a cake is cut into ten pieces of different sizes, is one piece a tenth? Why not?
phases.feels: one strip splitting into ten parts of exactly one width
phases.hands: Fold a paper strip in half, then fold and mark it until it has ten equal parts, and check them with a ruler. Colour one part and write what it is three ways: in words, as a fraction and as a decimal.
phases.tries: First rung: tap Cut and count the parts. Second rung: shade one part and read the fraction card. Third rung: the same task with the decimal card covered, reading the fraction first.

wrong.why: the strip looks ready to shade, and the cutting seems like an extra step
wrong.move: shades one part before tapping Cut, so the whole strip fills
wrong.screen: the whole strip fills deep blue and the decimal card reads one whole; the Cut button pulses once, and cutting splits the shading into ten shaded parts, all still counted

wrong.why: one part was shaded, so the number one feels like the answer
wrong.screen: the decimal card writes the digit after the point in amber and a 0 before it, and one whole strip is drawn beside the part strip so the two sizes are seen together

phases.screen: one whole strip, not yet cut, with the fraction card and the decimal card blank
phases.soWhat: one of ten equal parts is one tenth, 1/10 or 0.1

phases.win: nine parts shaded, 9/10 on one card and 0.9 on the other, with a 0 before the point for no whole ones
phases.does: shades parts one tap at a time and reads both cards after each tap
phases.goal: a number of tenths is written as a decimal with that digit after the point
phases.says: Each part you shade is one more tenth. Watch the digit after the point.
phases.check: Away from the screen: nine tenths of a strip is shaded. How many parts are not shaded, and what decimal names them?
phases.feels: the digit after the point ticking up with every part shaded
phases.hands: Colour some parts of a strip cut into ten, and write the fraction over ten. Then write the same amount as a decimal, with a 0 before the point and the count of coloured parts after it.
phases.tries: First rung: shade one part and read both cards. Second rung: shade one more and read them again. Third rung: the same task with the fraction card lit, before the decimal card is asked for.

wrong.why: the count is the number seen, and the point seems to go at the end
wrong.move: types the count of shaded parts before the point, as a whole number with a zero after it
wrong.screen: a whole strip for every unit the child typed is drawn beside the part strip, and the shaded run of the part strip is lit amber, so the two amounts stand side by side

wrong.why: both kinds of part are right there on the strip
wrong.move: counts the unshaded parts instead of the shaded ones
wrong.screen: each shaded part gets its own number in turn, from the left, and the unshaded parts stay warm white and unnumbered

phases.screen: one strip already cut into ten equal parts, with none shaded
phases.soWhat: a number of tenths is written as a decimal with that digit after the point

phases.win: the card reads 2.9 with Whole number part under the 2 and Decimal part under the 9
phases.does: shades tenths of the third strip and reads the decimal card, whole number part and decimal part
phases.goal: whole strips give the whole number part and the tenths give the decimal part, either side of the point
phases.says: The whole strips go before the point. The tenths go after it.
phases.check: Away from the screen: what does the digit before the point count, and what does the digit after it count?
phases.feels: the wholes and the tenths falling into place on either side of the point
phases.hands: Lay some whole paper strips end to end and one strip cut into tenths after them. Colour some tenths. Write the number of whole strips, a point, then the number of coloured tenths.
phases.tries: First rung: count the whole strips only. Second rung: count the shaded tenths only. Third rung: the same task with one whole strip, before more whole strips return.

wrong.why: both counts are part of the answer, and both feel like small numbers
wrong.move: writes the wholes and the tenths as one number after the point
wrong.screen: the whole strips light deep blue one by one and their count moves in front of the point on the decimal card, under the words Whole number part

wrong.why: the part strip is a strip too, so it seems to count as one
wrong.move: counts the part strip as one more whole
wrong.screen: the part strip's unshaded parts are lit amber, and the words Decimal part are drawn under its shaded run

phases.screen: two whole strips shaded, and a third strip cut into ten parts with none shaded
phases.soWhat: whole strips give the whole number part and tenths give the decimal part

phases.win: twenty-seven tenths close into two whole strips and seven tenths, and the card reads 2.7
phases.does: taps Lots of three times, trades each ten tenths for a whole strip, and reads what is left
phases.goal: ten tenths make one whole, so a count of tenths is read as ones and tenths
phases.says: Ten tenths fill a whole. Trade them, then count what is left.
phases.check: Away from the screen: how many whole strips can you make from forty-two tenths, and how many tenths are left?
phases.feels: ten loose tenths clicking together into one whole strip
phases.hands: Cut several strips into tenths and lay out a pile of loose tenths. Group them in tens and lay each ten along a whole strip. Count the whole strips and the tenths left over.
phases.tries: First rung: tap Lots of once and read the tally. Second rung: tap it again and trade any ten tenths. Third rung: the same task with fewer lots, before the full count returns.

wrong.why: the tally shows one number, and it looks like the answer
wrong.move: writes the count of tenths as a whole number
wrong.screen: the tally's tenths slide together ten at a time into whole strips, and the decimal card fills its two sides as they close

wrong.why: one trade feels like the whole job
wrong.move: stops trading after the first whole strip
wrong.screen: the loose tenths left over are counted aloud in tens, and each ten lights amber until it is traded

phases.screen: an empty strip cut into ten parts, the Lots of button set to nine tenths, and the Tenths tally at nothing
phases.soWhat: ten tenths make one whole, so a count of tenths is read as ones and tenths

writeup.delight: On the fourth phase, the moment the tenth part of a strip is shaded, the ten parts slide together with a soft click, their cut lines melt away, and the strip rises into the row of whole strips while the decimal card's whole number part ticks up by one.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing shaded yet. On the first phase one whole strip lies across the working area, not yet cut, with the fraction card and the decimal card blank beside it. On the second the strip is already cut into ten equal parts. On the third whole strips lie shaded above a part strip cut into tenths. On the fourth an empty part strip waits with the Lots of button set and the Tenths tally at nothing. One thing moves, once: the Cut button, or the first part of the strip, gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any number of strips, cut, shaded and traded, as strips or as circles, and the Lots of button set to any number of tenths. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on one tenth, tenths as decimals, wholes and tenths together, and counting tenths into ones.
voiceLines: A strip, waiting to be cut into ten equal parts.
Cut the strip into ten equal parts. Shade one. What is it called?
Each part you shade is one more tenth. Watch the digit after the point.
The whole strips go before the point. The tenths go after it.
Ten tenths fill a whole. Trade them, then count what is left.
A new strip. Check the parts are all one width.
Free play. Cut, shade and trade as many strips as you like.
Count the shaded parts again, one by one, and look at the point.
Ten tenths made a whole, and you counted every tenth.

observations.why: tenths come from cutting one whole into ten equal parts, and unequal pieces are not tenths.
observations.soWhat: one of ten equal parts is one tenth, 1/10 or 0.1.
observations.observe: The ten parts of a cut strip were all exactly one width.

observations.why: that digit counts tenths, and each part is one more tenth.
observations.soWhat: a number of tenths is written with that digit after the point.
observations.observe: Each tap on a part changed only the digit after the point.

observations.why: the point sits between the whole number part and the decimal part.
observations.soWhat: wholes go before the point and tenths go after it.
observations.observe: Whole strips changed the digit before the point, and part strips the digit after it.

observations.why: ten tenths fill exactly one whole.
observations.soWhat: a count of tenths is read as ones and tenths by trading each ten tenths for one whole.
observations.observe: Every time ten tenths were shaded, they closed into one whole strip.

description: Cut a strip into ten equal parts, shade tenths, read them as a fraction and a decimal, and watch ten tenths close into one whole.

mods.learn: Learn, adult alongside. Four worked items, one per phase, from one tenth of a strip to counting lots of tenths into ones and tenths.
mods.freeplay: Free Play. Any number of strips, the Cut, Shape, Trade and Lots of buttons, and the pad.

source_tool.name: Tenths Builder
source_tool.blurb: Cut a strip into ten equal parts, shade tenths, read them as a fraction and a decimal, and watch ten tenths close into one whole.

serves.exercise: finding how many grams of protein an adult needs each day at eight tenths of a gram for each kilogram
writing whole circles and a circle cut into tenths as a decimal
writing the shaded tenths of a bar, a grid, a circle and a decagon as a fraction and a decimal
writing six fractions with the denominator ten as decimals

source_tool.description: Strips of exactly one length lie across the working area, one under another, each labelled Whole at its left end. A Cut button splits the bottom strip into ten parts of equal width with near-black cut lines. A tap on a part shades it deep blue, and a second tap clears it. A fraction card and a decimal card sit to the right of the strips; the fraction card shows the shaded parts over ten and the decimal card shows the same amount with a large near-black point, turning green when the child's answer matches the shading. A Shape switch shows the same whole as a circle cut into ten equal sectors instead of a strip. Whole strips stack above the part strip, and the decimal card names Whole number part and Decimal part under its two sides. On the last phase a Trade button slides ten shaded tenths together, their cut lines fading to half strength, and closes them into one whole strip with a vermilion flash labelled Trade. A Lots of button adds the same number of tenths again each time it is tapped, and a Tenths tally counts every shaded tenth. A number pad sets any number of tenths up to ninety-nine. The running count at the top left of the canvas says how many tenths are shaded in all.
source_tool.art_direction: Paper strips cut into ten / Picture book

audio.note: Web Audio oscillators, no files. The same three cues in every tool of every Class 5 chapter, so the grade sounds like one grade.

wrong.note: A soft low double-bloop. A nudge, never a buzzer.

modes.note: THERE IS NO MODE AXIS ON THIS TOOL FAMILY. learn, practice and freeplay are gone and are not replaced by three of anything else: the axis itself is wrong for a tool a child works alone. See phase_mount.

authored.learn: Learn, adult alongside. Four worked items, one per phase, from one tenth of a strip to counting lots of tenths into ones and tenths.
authored.freeplay: Free Play. Any number of strips, the Cut, Shape, Trade and Lots of buttons, and the pad.
authored.practice: Practice, child alone. Eight items on tenths as fractions and decimals, wholes and tenths together, and trading ten tenths for one whole.

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: strips cut into ten equal parts, hundred grids of ten rows and ten columns, place value charts with a column for each place, column sums with their points in one line, and measuring jugs, ropes and scales marked in tenths.

Every whole is drawn the same size as every other whole it is compared or combined with, and its parts are exactly equal: a strip in tenths has ten parts of one width, and a hundred grid is always a full ten by ten.
The decimal point is drawn large and always sits between the ones and the tenths. In a column, every point lies on one vertical line.
A place value chart names every column above its digit: Hundreds, Tens, Ones, the point, Tenths, Hundredths, Thousandths.
Where shaded cells are counted, exactly the stated number is shaded, and they stay countable at a glance.

Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: a strip cutting into tenths, ten tenths sliding together into one whole, a zero appearing after the point, or a carry moving to the next place.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit or a part the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a decimal plays in a piece of working: every decimal or fraction the question gives is deep blue, with the shaded parts that show it, and every result the working reaches, a decimal, a fraction, a sum or a difference, is green, with its shaded parts; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Ten of one place traded for one of the next place, a carry in adding or a trade in taking away, is vermilion. A zero written at the end, after the point, to make like decimals is violet, and so is the point written after a whole number before those zeros. The part taken away, used or poured out is rose. The digit, place or step being worked on now, and the first place where two decimals differ, are amber. A zero holding a place open inside a number is grey. An unshaded part of a whole stays warm white inside its outline, and the decimal point itself is near-black ink. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Carry, Trade, Added zero, Taken away, Left and Place holder, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Count the shaded parts again, one by one, and look at the point.
voice.onNext: A new strip. Check the parts are all one width.
voice.opening: A strip, waiting to be cut into ten equal parts.
voice.onFinish: Ten tenths made a whole, and you counted every tenth.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Cut, shade and trade as many strips as you like.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: After the class has folded and cut a paper strip into ten equal parts and coloured some of them. The tool is what shades and counts a part at a time, and what slides ten tenths together into one whole, which cut paper can show only by being taped back up.

answer_key.rule: A whole cut into ten equal parts gives tenths. One part is one tenth, written 1/10 or 0.1. A number of tenths is written with that digit after the point. Whole strips give the whole number part, written before the point, and the tenths give the decimal part, written after it. 10 tenths make 1 whole, so a count of tenths is read as ones and tenths.
answer_key.wrong: The strips are shown again with every shaded part numbered in turn, and the child's answer is built as its own strip beside them, so the child sees whether the two shaded runs end in the same place. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The strip is cut into 10 equal parts, so each part is one tenth of the strip.
1 part is shaded, so the fraction is 1/10.
In decimal form one tenth is written 0.1: no whole ones, so 0 before the point, and 1 tenth after it.
It is read as zero point one.
items.answer: 1/10, which is written 0.1 and read as zero point one
items.question: A strip is cut into 10 equal parts and 1 part is shaded. Write the shaded part as a fraction and as a decimal.
items.checkpoint: One of ten equal parts is one tenth, 1/10 or 0.1.
items.misconception: Calling one part of a strip cut into unequal pieces a tenth, though tenths come only from ten equal parts.

steps: Each part is one tenth, and 8 parts are shaded, so 8 tenths are shaded.
There are no whole ones, so write 0 before the point.
The tenths digit comes straight after the point, so 8/10 = 0.8.
items.question: A strip is cut into 10 equal parts and 8 of them are shaded. Write the shaded part as a fraction and as a decimal.
items.checkpoint: The first digit after the point counts tenths.
items.misconception: Writing 8.0 for eight tenths, which puts the 8 in the ones place and means 8 whole strips.

steps: The 2 whole strips give the whole number part, 2.
The 9 tenths of the third strip give the decimal part, 9/10 or 0.9.
The point sits between the whole number part and the decimal part.
items.question: Two whole strips are shaded, and 9 tenths of a third strip. Write the shaded part as a decimal.
items.checkpoint: Whole strips go before the point and tenths go after it.
items.misconception: Writing 0.29 because 2 and 9 were both counted, though the 2 is whole strips and belongs before the point.

steps: 18 tenths and 9 tenths more make 27 tenths.
10 tenths make 1 whole, so 20 tenths make 2 wholes, and 7 tenths are left.
So 3 lots of 9 tenths is 27 tenths, which is 2.7.
items.answer: 27 tenths, which is 2 ones and 7 tenths, written 2.7
items.question: Count 3 lots of 9 tenths. How many ones and tenths is that? Write it as a decimal.
items.checkpoint: Count the tenths, then trade each ten tenths for one whole.
items.misconception: Writing 27 as the answer, which counts the tenths as if each one were a whole.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: A strip is cut into 10 equal parts. How many of the parts make the whole strip, and what is one part called?
items.final_answer: All 10 parts make the whole strip, and one part is one tenth, 1/10

items.question: How is 0.8 read, and what fraction is it?
items.final_answer: Zero point eight. It is 8 tenths, 8/10

items.question: Five whole strips are shaded, and 1 tenth of a sixth strip. Write the shaded part as a decimal.
In 7.9, what is the whole number part and what is the decimal part?
items.final_answer: The whole number part is 7 and the decimal part is 9 tenths

items.question: How many ones and tenths are 53 tenths? Write it as a decimal.
Count 4 lots of 6 tenths. Write the answer as a decimal.
items.final_answer: 24 tenths, which is 2 ones and 4 tenths, written 2.4

items.question: How many tenths are there in 6.1?
items.final_answer: 61 tenths: 6 wholes are 60 tenths, and 1 tenth more makes 61

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: splits the bottom strip, or circle, into ten equal parts
shades a part deep blue, or clears it on a second tap
shows the same whole as a strip or as a circle of ten equal sectors
slides ten shaded tenths together and closes them into one whole strip
adds the same number of tenths again each time it is tapped
sets a number of tenths up to ninety-nine, or types a fraction or a decimal

teaching_notes: Cut a paper strip into ten equal parts before any decimal is written, and check the parts are one width. Say each amount three ways, in words, as a fraction and as a decimal. Point at the decimal point every time and name the whole number part and the decimal part. Trade ten tenths for one whole on the desk before the tool does it. The opening box's question is counted in tenths the same way; leave that count to the child, with the box's own numbers, and do not work it for them. Multiplying decimals comes later.
generation_prompt: Build a tenths tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. Strips of exactly one length lie across the working area, one under another, each labelled Whole. A Cut button splits the bottom strip into ten parts of equal width; a tap shades a part deep blue and a second tap clears it. A fraction card and a decimal card sit to the right; the decimal card shows a large point and turns green when the answer matches, with Whole number part and Decimal part named under its two sides. A Shape switch shows the same whole as a circle of ten equal sectors. A Trade button slides ten shaded tenths together into one whole strip with a vermilion flash labelled Trade. A Lots of button adds the same number of tenths again each tap, and a Tenths tally counts them. A number pad sets up to ninety-nine tenths. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the number of shaded tenths. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Cut the strip into ten equal parts. Shade some parts. Read them as a fraction and as a decimal. When ten tenths are shaded, trade them for one whole.
